comments.author: tom@lant.uk
comments.text:
Good instinct to flag this. Based on how these proxies (jira-proxy.js, salesforce-proxy.js) are written, there are two concrete gaps
    relative to what you're hoping is already true:

    1. They're not actually localhost-only right now. They're started with http.createServer(...).listen(PORT, callback) — no host argument.
       Node's default when you omit the host is to bind 0.0.0.0, i.e. all network interfaces, not just the loopback interface. So as
       written, anything else on your LAN that can reach your machine's IP on that port could hit it — this isn't just a "hopefully"
       situation, it's actually open beyond localhost today. The fix is to pass the host explicitly: .listen(PORT, '127.0.0.1', callback).
    2. CORS is wide open: both set Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *, meaning any page loaded in the same browser — not just wigwag.html — can
       make a cross-origin fetch to http://localhost:8934/:8936 and pull data through it, if it can guess the endpoint shape (which isn't
       secret — it's public in this repo). That's a real vector even with correct localhost-only binding, since a malicious or compromised
       tab running in your own browser is still "local" from the proxy's point of view.

    Beyond fixing #1, a few things worth layering on:

    - Tighten CORS to the actual origin wigwag is served from instead of * — trickier if you open wigwag.html via file:// (origin comes
      through as null), but still narrows the surface for the common case of serving it over http.
    - A shared-secret header: have wigwag's Settings hold a token that gets sent on every proxy request, and have the proxy reject anything
      without it. This is the strongest single addition, because it defends against the "other local process/rogue tab" case that
      localhost-only binding alone doesn't cover — binding restricts network origin, not same-machine origin.
    - Minimize the exposure window: only run the proxy while you're actually linking things, then kill it, rather than leaving it up
      indefinitely.
    - One thing already done reasonably well: the startup/status logging only ever prints the auth mode (token / password-flow), never the
      actual credentials or fetched record contents — so at least nothing sensitive is landing in a terminal scrollback or log file by
      default.

    The localhost-binding fix (#1) is the one I'd treat as not-optional — it's a real, currently-open gap, not a hypothetical one.

comments.text: Fixed in b2179db. Root cause: renderVals() recomputed the sort live on every render, so editing a field in the currently-sorted column (e.g. Status/RAG) moved the row the instant the edit committed -- it visibly vanished from under the cursor mid-click. Now the row order is snapshotted right before a same-column edit commits and held for a short grace period, so the edit's new value shows in place first; the table settles into the real sorted order once the grace period elapses. An explicit re-sort/clear/project-switch drops the freeze immediately. New regression coverage in tests/interaction.spec.js.

comments.text: Follow-up: found a gap in this fix while testing the new "clear a select field" feature -- sortSnapshot (the frozen order) was only ever computed by an explicit sortBy()/switchProject() call, never at initial page load. A fresh load with an already-persisted sort preference (the common case: sorted in an earlier session, then just reopened the tab) fell through to the live/unfrozen sort branch until the next explicit re-sort, reproducing the original jarring reorder on the very first edit. Fixed: sortSnapshot is now also computed once at boot, right after the initial project's issues load.

Root cause: publishGithubLeaderStatus() kept heartbeating leadership even while its own tab was backgrounded, so a stale/forgotten hidden tab could hold the sync-leader claim indefinitely -- only the leader polls, and a hidden leader's own poll always no-ops by design, so remote changes stopped being picked up at all, silently. comments.author: claude@lant.uk
comments.text:
Root-caused and fixed. startMerge() is the single real merge function every caller goes through, but the GitHub sync path (connectGithubRepo, pollGithubForRemoteChanges) never checked whether a fetched file's own declared projectId matched the project it was being merged into -- and both are async functions that never re-checked state.projectId after their awaits either. Switching projects while a connect/poll was still in flight could apply a stale result (the merge itself, sha/etag bookkeeping, sync status) to whatever project happened to be active by the time it resolved.

Confirmed via a git-stash A/B that this reproduces the real reported bug exactly: reverting just the fix leaks a synced project's full issue list into a brand-new blank project when the connect resolves mid-switch.

Two independent layers now in place: (1) startMerge() itself refuses to merge content whose own declared projectId doesn't match the active project (the one legitimate caller that deliberately merges a foreign-declared file after an explicit user confirm -- Apply update's mismatch dialog -- opts out via a new allowProjectMismatch flag); (2) connectGithubRepo/pollGithubForRemoteChanges/pushToGithub each capture their project id up front and re-check it after every await.

Landed as commit 42e1019, with two new regression tests in tests/github-sync.spec.js. Full suite passes (500/500, only the two pre-existing KNOWN GAP staleness tests show their usual soft-fail marker). Related to #43/#45 (same GitHub-sync area, same session).

Fixed: node wigwag-cli.js's main() now pulls remote changes first (best-effort) before list/show/add-issue/comment/set-field -- the exact commands that previously had no reason to ever notice the remote moved since the last pull. pull/push/sync were untouched since they already sync as part of what they do (an extra pre-pull there would've just been a redundant network round-trip).

history.value:
I like the direction, but "notifications on change" is necessary and not sufficient — a few other pieces need to exist before conversations can actually live in tickets rather than just being logged there:

Notifications themselves — wigwag has no push/poll-to-user channel today; the GitHub sync layer polls GitHub, but nothing watches the local tracker and tells a human "something changed." You'd need either a lightweight watcher (desktop notification, email, Slack webhook) triggered off the signed-history append, or a digest/mention model so people aren't pinged on every field edit — just comments and @-mentions aimed at them.

@-mentions and a notion of "who's this comment for." Comments today are just history entries — nobody is addressed. Real conversation needs a way to say "this needs Thomas" vs "just a log entry," or every comment becomes a notification to everyone watching the issue.

Read/unread state per user. Otherwise every reopen of an issue looks unchanged-vs-new the same way, and conversation threads become unnavigable once they're more than a couple comments deep.

Faster round-trip than the current GitHub-sync path. Right now writes go through a push-debounce and conditional-polling pull cycle — fine for backlog grooming, way too laggy for back-and-forth conversation. Real-time-feeling chat needs either a much shorter poll interval or a proper push channel (websocket/SSE) rather than the current ETag-polling model.

Threading/reply structure, since comments are currently a flat append-only log — fine for a decision trail, less fine for "which of these three points are you responding to" once a conversation gets going.

I'd treat notifications as the trigger that makes this worth doing at all, but mentions + read state are what actually make it usable as a conversation medium rather than a fancy activity log.

comments.author: claude@lant.uk
comments.text:
Design sketch: instead of a live chat session driving Claude Code work, wigwag issues become the sole decision channel -- Tom files/comments on issues, Claude periodically checks the tracker and acts.

Scoping (for now): an issue with Status = "Next" is in Claude's scope to pick up and act on. Nothing else -- Todo/In Progress/Blocked/Done/Won't Do issues are never touched autonomously, only ones Tom has explicitly promoted to Next. In the fullness of time this probably wants a real Assignee field instead (so scoping isn't overloaded onto the same field that also tracks workflow state), but Status=Next is sufficient to start.

Loop mechanism: Claude Code's own ScheduleWakeup dynamic-loop primitive, checking on a slow cadence (20-30 min, matching wigwag-agent.js's own ~10-20s-per-call cost against a real shared tracker with other concurrent editors) -- not a tight loop.

Per-issue flow once picked up: Claude moves Status to "In Progress" (visible signal it's being worked, and removes it from the next poll's Next-scan), does the work, comments on the issue with what it did (same pattern as the mention-notification comment on #70 this session), then moves Status to "Done" -- or "Blocked" with a comment explaining what it's blocked on, if it can't proceed without Tom's input. Tom's replies/comments on a Blocked or even Done issue while Claude is between polls are how follow-up direction gets back in, without ever needing a live chat session.

Needed pieces:
- A polling script (list issues where Status==Next, scoped to this project) -- built as part of this issue, using wigwag-client.js's list() which already resolves Status labels.
- The ScheduleWakeup loop wiring to actually run this on a cadence.
- Judgment calls each iteration still needs a real Claude Code turn (reading the issue, deciding how to act) -- the polling script only answers "is there work," it doesn't do the work itself.

Safety: this is a live, shared tracker other real users edit (per this repo's own CLAUDE.md) -- scope is deliberately narrow (Status=Next only, never proactively touching other issues/other users' items) to keep blast radius small while this is being trialled.

comments.author: claude@lant.uk
comments.text:
You're right that email and key aren't entangled -- that's by design, and it's already written down in docs/FORMAT.md's 'Identity and signing' section: 'This is explicitly not a security boundary. The email is self-proclaimed, not verified by any authority... a lightweight who-did-this-and-was-it-tampered-with mechanism for collaborators who are basically trusting each other already.' The signature's real job is tamper-evidence (did this entry's content change after it was signed), not authentication (is this really that person).

Interesting finding: the docs (and a code comment in wigwag-core.js) already describe an intended answer to your exact question -- a TOFU (trust-on-first-use) identity store that remembers which pubkey an email used first, and flags a LATER import claiming the same email with a DIFFERENT key as 'a possible impersonation attempt'. But I checked, and it's not actually wired up anywhere -- verifyPayload() is imported into wigwag.html's Component class but never once called. So today, literally nothing checks key-per-email consistency at all; the docs describe a plan that was never implemented.

Given that gap, I'd actually caution against implementing TOFU exactly as documented, because of the exact scenario you raised: since multi-device use is common, and each device/browser generates its own key independently the first time it's opened, strict TOFU would false-positive constantly -- your own laptop and phone, both legitimately you, would look like 'impersonation' to each other the moment their data merges, since each device's local TOFU store only ever saw ITS OWN key as tom@lant.uk's 'first' one.

My recommendation: don't try to pin one key per email at all. Keep email as the human-facing attribution/grouping label (already true everywhere), and let pubKey mean 'which device/session produced this', full stop -- multiple legitimate keys per email is the normal case, not an anomaly to flag. If you want SOME visibility here later, I'd suggest something soft and informational rather than a security alarm -- e.g. a project could note 'tom@lant.uk has signed from 3 different keys' as a fact, not a warning -- but I wouldn't build even that without a concrete reason it'd help, given the doc's own explicit stance that this was never meant to resist a motivated adversary. Filed the soft/informational version as a separate backlog item (not Next) in case you want to revisit it later -- this issue's core question feels answered as 'no action needed, current behavior is fine and matches the documented intent once you drop the never-implemented TOFU-alarm idea'.

comments.text:
Fixed: the Notification API's own `tag` option now dedupes this at the browser level -- new Notification(title, { body, tag: 'wigwag-mention-' + commentId }) in checkForNewMentions. Two independent fire attempts for the same comment (from two tabs racing, or a same-tab retry) share the same tag, so the OS replaces rather than stacks them -- only one visible notification ever, regardless of timing.

This is a different, narrower layer than NOTIFIED_MENTIONS_KEY (the existing localStorage-based 'have we told the user about this' set): that already prevents re-notifying about the same comment on a LATER poll, but it's a check-then-act read+write with no cross-tab locking, so two tabs polling independently (no leader election, by design) could both decide 'not yet notified' in the same race window before either writes back. The tag fix closes exactly that gap natively, without needing any actual cross-tab coordination/locking.

Covered by a new test in tests/mentions.spec.js asserting the tag is derived from the comment's own id, plus a direct simulation of a second near-simultaneous fire collapsing into the same notification. Full suite: 606/606 passing.
